desc:
A number is upside-down symmetric if it reads the same after the paper is rotated by 180 degrees. Under that rotation the digits 0, 1 and 8 stay the same, 6 becomes 9 and 9 becomes 6, and no other digit is allowed. The rotated number is read in the opposite order, so 69, 88, 96 and 609 qualify, while 25 and 962 do not. Numbers are written without leading zeros, and 0 itself is upside-down symmetric.

Count the upside-down symmetric integers x with low ≤ x ≤ high.

Example: low = 50, high = 100 gives 3 (69, 88 and 96).
hints: The range can be two billion numbers wide, so you cannot test every number. But there are very few upside-down symmetric numbers.

Such a number is built from the outside in: the first and last digit are a pair (0-0, 1-1, 8-8, 6-9 or 9-6), the next two digits are the next pair, and so on. An odd length has a middle digit that is 0, 1 or 8.

Generate all of them for every length from the number of digits of low up to the number of digits of high, never put 0 as the outer digit of a number longer than one digit, and count those that lie in the range.
editorial: Let build(L, outer) return all symmetric digit strings of length L. For L = 0 it is the empty string, for L = 1 it is 0, 1 and 8, and otherwise wrap every string of length L - 2 with one of the five digit pairs. The flag outer forbids the pair 0-0 at the outermost level so that no number has a leading zero (the single digit 0 is still allowed).

There are only 4 * 5(L/2) - 1 such numbers of an even length L and 4 * 5(L-3)/2 * 3 of an odd length L, so about 5,000 numbers of up to ten digits in total. Generate each length between the digit counts of low and high and count the ones that fall in [low, high]; the lengths strictly between the two end lengths are inside the range automatically, but a simple comparison on each generated value is just as good.
time: O(number of symmetric numbers with up to 10 digits)
